extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors seeking literary agents / writers preparing query letters for traditional publishing
extracted.subtask_description: A how-to rubric for composing a four-part query letter (subject line, personalized intro, hook, comps, bio, sign-off) aimed at landing literary-agent interest and manuscript requests. Focused on fiction query letters illustrated with examples and dos/don'ts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query letter subject line format
rubrics_metrics.description: Your Query Letter Subject Line: You want this to read Query for: and then the literary agent's name, your book title in all caps, and, in parentheses, your genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example format given in the post. Use exactly 'Query for:' followed by the agent's name, the BOOK TITLE IN ALL CAPS, and (genre) in parentheses so the agent immediately knows what you're pitching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalized intro / agent-specific fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Start by personalizing the query to the literary agent and letting them know that you're not just mass bcc-ing a bunch of agents. Show that you did your homework and you really think this particular agent is a good fit for your book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention an author or a book the agent has repped, or a part of their wish list and why your book would be a good fit. Note: personalization can be placed at the bottom of the letter as well, but it must be included somewhere. Anti-pattern: generic or copy-pasted intros—agents are 'flooded' and small deviations from the norm can be red flags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition/offer line
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a quick transition line offering your work for consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a concise line such as “I would love to offer WE SHIP IT for your consideration.” This signals immediately what you're pitching and moves into the pitch portion of the letter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hook: purpose and length
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hook is the core pitch that 'hooks' the agent — it should pitch the book, give enough descriptive information to be clear, and leave the agent intrigued and wanting more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the hook generally around 150 to 200 words max. Don't try to include every element of the book; synthesize into a compelling summary (like a back-cover blurb). The main goal is to get the agent to request the full manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hook first line / inciting incident
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important part of your hook is the first line; often include or lead up to the inciting incident of your book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example first line from the post: 'The last place type-A overachiever Olivia Schwartz wants to be is on a cruise.' The inciting incident should be 'earth-shattering' for the protagonist (even if not world-shattering) because it justifies the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define the main character's 'old world' / stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Include background info about the current state of your main character's life before the inciting incident so the agent understands why the event is impactful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide revealing details that make the stakes clear (example: family dynamics, prior trauma). Keep it concise — just enough context so the inciting incident 'lands.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Show the main character's plan / goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Convey what the protagonist is trying to do (their plan) in the face of the new situation, to define character and stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Olivia plans to spend the week holed up in her cabin with her research and her highlighters in her quest to get chosen for a prestigious medical internship.' Use this to reveal character traits and priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include conflict (early and clear)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the query includes conflict: a game-changing obstacle or complication (often appearing around a quarter/third of the way through the story) that sets the plot in motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You don't need to summarize the entire plot, but signal the first or key conflicts (example: meeting a love interest who is 'everything Olivia's not'). Avoid spoilers but make clear what's at stake and who/what opposes the protagonist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create an emotional heartbeat
rubrics_metrics.description: Show why events matter emotionally for the main character — this 'secret sauce' makes the query resonate and makes agents care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie events back to the character's interior life or emotional wounds (example: 'For the first time since her brother died seven years ago, Olivia feels like she can have fun.'). The emotional core is what makes readers want more.

rubrics_metrics.name: End the hook with intrigue
rubrics_metrics.description: Finish the hook by hinting at larger problems or consequences without giving everything away; leave the agent wanting to read the full manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End with lines that show 'there's a lot more to this book' and avoid rhetorical questions or confusing statements. Example closing: 'But there's a lot bubbling up under the surface on this cruise... Olivia must face all the truths that she's ignored for so long.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Include strong comps (two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include two comp titles (books or other media) that show where your book would sit on bookstore shelves and what it shares in tone, theme, or setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your book shouldn't be identical to the comps, but they should have something in common. Comps can be placed either before or after the hook. Use comps to demonstrate market placement and reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short, relevant author bio
rubrics_metrics.description: Finish with a brief one- or two-line bio: list prior publications if you have them and include one or two interesting details, especially those that relate to why you're the right person to tell this story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't worry if you have no prior publications; focus on interesting, relevant details. Example: mention degrees or life experiences that inform your storytelling ('graduated with a degree in love' / founded a matchmaking startup).

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendly, concise sign-off
rubrics_metrics.description: Close the letter with a brief, friendly sign-off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the tone professional but warm. The post demonstrates a short, courteous closing as part of a polished query letter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise with broad feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Get lots of feedback and keep improving your query letter before sending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send drafts to friends and family, people on social media, readers who have read your book and those who haven't. Iteration and external feedback are emphasized as crucial to perfecting the query.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deviations and unprofessional submission behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Small deviations from the query-letter norm can be red flags to agents; don't mass BCC and don't present a query that looks mass-sent or careless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents are 'flooded' with queries; professionalism, adherence to norms, and clear personalization reduce the chance your letter is discarded. Be cautious about over- or under-informing—don't confuse the agent or try to cram too much in.
